opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's been humbling. A few years ago, if you'd asked me when we'd see video models that could produce minute-long clips with consistent characters, plausible lighting, and objects that mostly obey physics, I would have given you a much longer timeline. I come from robotics, where progress feels slow and hard-won. You fight for every percentage point of success rate on a real robot, so my instincts were calibrated to that pace.

What surprised me most wasn't the visual quality. I expected that to keep improving with scale. It was how much implicit physical understanding seemed to emerge from training on enormous amounts of video. Things like how cloth drapes, how liquid pours, how a person's weight shifts when they walk. Nobody hand-coded those dynamics, yet the models capture a surprising amount of them. For someone who spent years building physics simulators to train robots, that was a real "wait a minute" moment.

That said, I try to stay calibrated. These models still make mistakes that reveal they don't truly understand causality. Objects appear or disappear, hands do strange things, and interactions fall apart over longer horizons. Looking good to a human viewer and being accurate enough for a robot to plan with are very different bars. So I'd say my expectations were challenged on the upside for perceptual realism, while the deeper question, whether these become reliable world models we can act on, is still open. That's exactly what makes it so exciting to work on right now.

r001.rationale: He says he would have expected minute-long video-generation clips with consistent characters and plausible scenes to arrive much later, acknowledging he underestimated the timeline.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's humbled me more than once. When I started working in this space, my mental model was that video was going to be the hard frontier for a long time, because you're not just modeling pixels, you're modeling physics, continuity, causality across time. Early results had that uncanny quality, objects melting into each other, hands with seven fingers, people walking backwards while appearing to walk forward. I remember telling people that getting to even ten seconds of coherent, physically plausible video would take years of fundamental breakthroughs.

And then, within what felt like a few months, we were seeing minute-long clips with consistent characters, plausible lighting, water that actually behaved like water. What surprised me wasn't just the quality, it was how much of it came from scaling and from reframing the problem, treating video as a world simulator rather than as a sequence of images. That reframing unlocked a lot more than I expected.

So I've had to recalibrate how I think about timelines. My instinct now is to assume that if something looks like it's two years away, it may be six months away, and to spend less energy predicting and more energy thinking about what we do once it arrives. The hard problems have shifted too. It's less about whether the model can produce something beautiful and more about control, consistency over long horizons, and whether it truly understands the world or is just very good at mimicking its surface. Those questions are still open, and that's what keeps it interesting.

r001.rationale: He says he expected coherent, plausible video to take years, then saw major progress within months, and describes having to recalibrate his timelines.

astra-6.text:
It has moved faster than I expected. I used to think of video generation as a series of separate challenges: first getting individual frames to look good, then making motion coherent, then maintaining consistency over time. What surprised me is how much progress could happen across those dimensions together.

At the same time, a compelling clip and a system you can reliably control are different milestones. Can you get the exact motion you want? Can you change one detail without changing everything else? Those questions make me cautious about predicting what comes next. The pace has pushed me to update my expectations more frequently, while looking carefully at what the models can do consistently.

sol-6.1.text:
It’s been faster than I expected. What surprised me most is not just the improvement in visual quality, but how quickly these models have become better at maintaining motion and coherence over time. You see a result and think, “That would have seemed very difficult a year ago,” and then, a few months later, it starts to feel normal.

But I think there’s still a gap between generating something that looks plausible and really understanding how the world works. From a robotics perspective, that’s a particularly interesting question: can these models predict what happens when you take an action, including when something unexpected occurs? The progress makes me optimistic, but it also makes me more careful about assuming where the limits are.
